Title: LSJ: Playing to Win & Honoring Deals (or not)

Messages.Author: extrala
Messages.Body:
Yet another playing to win thread (or at least sort of) ...

During the tournament during the last weekend I encountered the
following situation:

The four player table is set up like this: Peter --> Axel --> Ralf -->
John

Ralf puts too much pressure on John early on, so John proposes the
following deal to Peter. John just wants one VP (which is reasonable
in his position), while Peter takes the GW. Peter accepts, and now the
following happens. Peter ousts Axel and Ralf in quick succession, and
then puts John down to one pool (who has no controlled minion), while
exhausting his library. Instead of bleeding him out, Peter chooses to
withdraw, and makes the game win by that (with 2.5 VP).

So my question is, was that a legal play? The judge (tournament
organizer) rule it was.

My objection is that by choosing to withdraw, Peter's either not
playing to win (he does not have the game win in that situation yet),
or much more importantly, Peter's honoring the deal, although all
deals are off in the heads-up.

The counter argument was, that Peter has 2 VPs and is free to make the
decision how he's making the game win (by ousting John or
withdrawing).

If the answer is, that the play was legal, then I would strongly like
to see the tournament rules changed, so that you have to maximize your
VPs, instead of "only" going for the game win. I was under the
impression, that the changes to the tournament rules (in 2008?) was
implemented to avoid this kind of table-split deals.

Best regards, Ralf

The question of honoring a deal only comes up when the activity in
question is not PTW on its own. In this case, the activity is PTW on
its own, so it doesn't matter if the PTW activity would also have been
in keeping with the no-longer-existant deal.

> The counter argument was, that Peter has 2 VPs and is free to make the
> decision how he's making the game win (by ousting John or
> withdrawing).

This is correct.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
extrala <ralf.l...@gmx.de> wrote:
>As stated before, then I strongly suggest that maximizing one's VP
>(regardless if you have (or will get) the GW) should be part of the
>VEKN tournament rules, in order to fix this loophole (at least from my
>point of view) in the tournament rules.

Such a rules change has potential collateral damage that you would need
to carefully examine.

In particular, it means that players can and should prevent cross-table
ousts on a table. *Any* oust by another player means that your Game Win
will not be a sweep. Therefore, to maximize your VPs with your Game
Win, everyone else has to still be in the game. Of course, the other
players will think similarly. This can lead to a flurry of defensive
action and stagnation - in a close game, potentially none of the players
who think they can win the table can allow anyone to be ousted and must
vote to save a player, and so on.

Certainly, there are players who will aim for a sweep anyway - it's a
good thing! - but they are not bound by the rules to do so, and there is
no way for another player to get the judge to force such a course of
behaviour. ("But judge, he *has* to save me in this vote, or else he
won't get the sweep.")

This is similar to some of the consequences that would be brought about
by forcing players to maximize TPs (which they don't have to), or
forcing a player to follow a particular course of action when in a lost
position.

--
James Coupe

I still do not get why you are upset about this. The new rules were
implemented to force players not to loose the game/forfeit the GW in a
heads up situation because of a previously made deal. This was done to
prevent the very early (in the game) split deals we were seeing back in
the day, which were frustrating for the other players. The new rules
were never made to shut down VP deals entirely and force players to
maximize VPs under all circumstances disregarding the spirit of
previously made arrangments, which is a good thing since arrangements
are part of this game. This is and has always been a social game, even
if some people want it to be a card-slappers game.
